PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Balance — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches balance as a quiet body conversation: arms out, eyes on the end of the line, feet talking to the ears — one slow chalk-line walk at a time.

What is this?

Balance is staying steady when the ground narrows or the body wobbles: the ears read the tilt, the eyes pick a target, the legs correct. Three helpers, one steady walk.

What does it mean?

Balance is the base under every other playground skill — the swing mount, the ladder climb, the hop all start with a moment of steadiness. It is also the quietest skill here: the body goes still to get better.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three balance ideas: arms out are the wings — wide arms widen the wobble-margin; eyes pick a FIXED point ahead — looking down at the feet tips the body; slow beats fast — the slower the step, the longer the ears have to correct.

Why this matters

Of the fifteen action words, balance is the one that quietly trains the others: the steadier the base, the braver the jump, the swing and the climb.

What it teaches

Static and dynamic balance, ear-eye-leg coordination, focus (fixed-point gazing), and self-calming — a balance walk is deep-breathing in disguise.

Words to learn

balancesteadywobblearms outslowkerbtightrope

Say this to your child

“"Balance is steady feet on a narrow line! Arms out like airplane wings, eyes on the tree at the end — not your feet — and step… so… slowly. The slower you go, the more your body can catch you. Wobbles are allowed — every wobble is your body practising its comeback!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is balance — steady feet on a narrow line."
  2. Wings first: arms out wide — "airplane wings keep you up." Demonstrate the difference: arms in (wobbly), arms out (steady).
  3. Eyes ahead: pick a target at the end of the line — "your eyes steer your feet." Practise looking ahead, not down.
  4. The slow walk: chalk line, kerb or bench edge — step… step… step. Slow is the skill; speed comes on its own.
  5. Play the tightrope games below and close: "wings out, eyes ahead, slow steps."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Balance" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly balancing illustration below — exactly as the steady pose looks.

Ask your child

"Where do the arms go? Where do the eyes look — feet or ahead? What happens when we go slower?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Airplane wings out!" "My eyes steer my feet!" or the wobble report: "I wobbled three times and caught myself!"

Out in the real world

Balance lines are everywhere: kerbs, garden edges, painted lines, the shadow of a fence. Any walk becomes a tightrope when a line appears — the skill travels home free.

Try it together

Tightrope Progression: chalk line forwards, then backwards, then sideways — three walks, each slower than the last. Then the beanbag ride: walk the line with a beanbag on the head — the bag only stays when the steps are truly steady. Count the wobbles together across the week and watch them shrink. Wings out, eyes ahead — the tightrope is anywhere.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do the arms do? Where do the eyes look? Does slow or fast win?" Wings out, ahead, slow — three answers and the line is walked.

Parent tips

Chalk before kerbs, kerbs before benches: raise the line’s height only when the floor version looks easy. And count wobbles as wins — the counting makes practice into a game, not a test.

This lesson pairs with the Balance flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Catch — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches catching in its right order: the EYES catch the ball first, the hands just finish the job — a watching skill wearing gloves.

What is this?

Catch is stopping a flying thing with the hands: eyes track the ball, hands move to the spot, fingers close around it — a soft cage, not a hard slap.

What does it mean?

Every failed beginner catch is a watching failure: the hands close where the ball WAS. Teaching eyes-first reframes catching from a grab into a tracking game, and tracking is trainable with balloons.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three catch ideas: the eyes catch the ball — hands just close where the eyes say; the catch is a soft cage — big hands, bent elbows, ball pulled IN as it arrives; and starting big — balloons and slow rolls — beats starting small and hard.

Why this matters

Catching is the confidence keystone of ball play: children who catch relax into every throwing, batting and team game that follows.

What it teaches

Eye tracking, hand-eye timing, soft-hands catching (the pull-in), and gentle bravery — a ball coming AT you asks for calm, not flinch.

Words to learn

catchwatchtracksoft handscageballoonready

Say this to your child

“"Catch is a watching game! Your eyes grab the ball first — follow it, follow it — and your hands just close where your eyes say: a big soft cage, fingers wide, and pull it IN gently. Balloons first, balls later: whatever flies, you catch it with your eyes first!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is catch — two hands close around a flying ball."
  2. Eyes first: roll a ball slowly and let your child WATCH it all the way into still hands — the roll cannot miss. "Your eyes caught it before your hands did!"
  3. The cage: arms out, elbows bent, fingers spread — a big bird cage. Ball arrives; fingers close, hands pull gently IN — hugging the ball, not slapping it.
  4. Balloon rounds: balloons hang long enough for tracking to win — ten catches, no flinches.
  5. Play the catch games below and close: "watch it all the way in."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Catch" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly catching illustration below — exactly as the two-hand cage looks.

Ask your child

"What catches the ball first? What shape do the hands make? Do we slap the ball or pull it in?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My eyes caught it!" "A soft bird cage!" or the proud count: "Ten balloon catches — no drops!"

Out in the real world

Catch practice lives in every garden and hallway — and the tracking game lives everywhere: follow a soap bubble, a falling leaf, a soap bubble of a balloon. Eyes first, hands second — for life.

Try it together

Roll-and-Catch Ladder: level one, sitting, rolling a ball back and forth — pure tracking. Level two, standing, gentle underarm tosses at chest height — cage closes. Level three, balloons — slower, higher, funnier. Level four, small soft ball with a bounce in between. Each level is one game day; the ladder climbs on confidence, not age.

Understanding check

Ask: "What catches first? What shape are the hands? Slap or pull?" The eyes, a soft cage, pull — three answers and the ball is yours.

Parent tips

Keep tosses at CHEST height — rising balls vanish over the head and scare beginners. And say "watch it all the way in" every round: the phrase does the coaching.

This lesson pairs with the Catch flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Climb — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches climbing the way playground teachers wish every child learned it: three points touching, legs doing the pushing, and the down-climb respected as much as the up.

What is this?

Climbing is going up using hands and feet together: grip with the hands, push with the legs, and keep three of the four touching the ladder or frame while one limb moves.

What does it mean?

The three-point rule is climbing’s safety spine — one move at a time, three holds always. And the down-climb is the hidden curriculum: children who practise coming down carefully never make the panicked drop.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three climb ideas: three points touch while ONE moves — count them out loud; the legs PUSH more than the arms pull — strong climber legs; and down is climbed, not jumped — feet find the rung below by looking.

Why this matters

Climbing builds grip, sequencing and nerve — and the three-point habit, learned at two on a low ladder, is the same habit that keeps five-year-olds sensible on the high frame.

What it teaches

Alternating grip strength, cross-lateral stepping, rule-keeping under excitement, and the down-skill — planning the descent.

Words to learn

climbgripthree pointsrungdownsteadyup

Say this to your child

“"Climbing is hands and feet together up the ladder — with the three-point rule! Three points always touch: two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand — and only ONE limb moves at a time. Your legs do the pushing, your hands do the gripping. And coming down? Down is climbed too — slower than up!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is climb — up the ladder with hands and feet together."
  2. Three points: hands and feet on the ladder — count them: one hand, two hands, one foot, two feet… FOUR points! Now move ONE — three points stay. That is the rule.
  3. Legs push: the arms grip, the LEGS lift — "your legs are the strong ones." Practise a step where the foot does the work.
  4. The count-climb: climb slowly, saying "three points… move… three points… move."
  5. Practise the DOWN slowly too, then play the climb games below: "up slow, down slower."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Climb" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly climbing illustration below — exactly as the ladder climb looks.

Ask your child

"How many points stay touching? Which muscles push — arms or legs? How do we come down — jump or climb?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Three points touch!" "My legs are the strong ones!" or the down-climber: "Down slower than up!"

Out in the real world

Climbing frames, ladders, stairs and big couches — the three-point rule transfers to every one. Count the points on the stairs tonight: the habit walks home.

Try it together

Count-Climb Ladder: a low ladder or playground rungs. Climb up with the count out loud — "three points… move… three points" — then climb DOWN with the same count, feet finding each rung by looking. Then the soft-step game: from the lowest rung, place both feet back on the ground one at a time — no jumps, just placement. Up slow, down slower: the rule that grows with the frame.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many points touch? What do the legs do? Jump or climb down?" Three, push, climb — three answers and the ladder is safe.

Parent tips

Stay below and slightly behind on early climbs — a spotting shadow, not a crane. And never rush the down: the child who can down-climb will never freeze at height.

This lesson pairs with the Climb flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Dig — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches digging as slow archaeology: the scoop, the pry, the pile — and the patience of going DEEPER instead of starting new holes everywhere.

What is this?

Dig is pulling the ground apart with hands or tools: scoop the sand, pry the gravel, pile it up, and keep going — down toward the treasure, the water table, or just the interesting dark layer.

What does it mean?

Digging is whole-body strength work disguised as treasure hunting: wrists scoop, arms pry, trunk stabilises. And its virtue is patience — one hole, going deeper, beats twelve holes, one inch each.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three dig ideas: the scoop is a wrist turn — fingers curl, wrist rolls the load out; the pry is a lever — wiggle the stick DOWN then lift; and deep beats wide — one hole with a mission beats a garden of scratches.

Why this matters

Digging builds grip, wrist rotation and trunk strength — the lifting muscles — while teaching the one-sitting virtue of sticking with a job that starts slow.

Words to learn

digscooppryspadepiledeeptreasure

Say this to your child

“"Digging is going DOWN — scoop the sand, pry the stones, pile it up, and keep going deeper! Curl your fingers and turn your wrist for the scoop. Push the stick down to pry the stone up — levers are magic. And the digger’s law: one deep hole beats twelve shallow ones. Deeper, deeper, treasure!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is dig — down to the treasure, one scoop at a time."
  2. The scoop: hands or spade — fingers curl under, wrist turns, load lifts, pile grows. Practise the wrist turn in the air first.
  3. The pry: a stick or spade tip under a stone — push DOWN on the handle, the stone lifts. Levers are magic with rules.
  4. The mission: pick ONE hole and dig it deeper each day — mark the depth with a stick. Deep beats wide!
  5. Play the dig games below and close: "scoop, pry, deeper."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Dig" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly digging illustration below — exactly as the spadeful looks.

Ask your child

"What does the wrist do in a scoop? How does the pry lift the stone? One deep hole or twelve shallow ones?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Wrist turn — scoop!" "The stone flew up — lever magic!" or the archaeologist: "My hole is deeper than yesterday!"

Out in the real world

Sandpits, gardens, the beach at low tide — digging jobs are everywhere, and so are the treasures: worms, shells, old coins of the playground. The pry is how real archaeologists lift every stone.

Try it together

Treasure Dig: bury three "treasures" (a bottle-cap coin, a marble, a shell) in a sandpit or a rice bin — one shallow, one middle, one DEEP. The mission: recover all three from ONE hole, using scoops and prys, marking depth with a stick. Finish with the museum: treasures displayed on a bench, hole solemnly refilled. Scoop, pry, deeper — the archaeologist’s whole day.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the wrist do? What lifts the stone? Deep or wide?" Turns, the pry, deep — three answers and the hole is going down.

Parent tips

Wet sand holds walls and teaches deep digging; dry sand teaches patience with collapse — both are honest teachers. And the refill is part of the game: diggers leave the ground as they found it.

This lesson pairs with the Dig flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Hide — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hiding as three quiet skills: get small, get silent, hold still — the most delicious self-control game ever invented.

What is this?

Hide is putting yourself or a thing where it cannot be seen: squeeze small, move quiet, then FREEZE — and the hiding is only as good as the stillness that follows.

What does it mean?

Hiding is self-control wearing a game: the urge to giggle, peek and dash is enormous, and holding still through it is a genuine regulation workout — the most fun a four-year-old will ever have doing nothing.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three hide ideas: get SMALL — curl, crouch, tuck into the space; get QUIET — quiet feet going out, no giggles on the way; and STILL is the third skill — the hider holds still until found, no matter the itch.

Why this matters

Hide-and-seek trains impulse control, spatial thinking (where would a seeker look first?) and the social joy of taking turns being lost and found — all in one game.

What it teaches

Self-control (stillness, silence), spatial perspective-taking (what can the seeker see?), quiet movement, and the emotional rollercoaster of being found.

Words to learn

hidesmallquietstillseekcountfound

Say this to your child

“"Hiding is three quiet skills! Get SMALL — curl up like a cat. Get QUIET — tip-toe feet, no giggles till you’re hidden. Then get STILL — a statue that cannot giggle, cannot wiggle, until you’re found! And being found is the best part: FOUND! — and now it’s your turn to seek."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is hide — small, quiet, and still!"
  2. Get small: curl behind a chair — knees up, arms in, a smaller shape than usual. Practise the curl.
  3. Get quiet: walk on quiet feet to the spot — tip-toes, no giggles UNTIL hidden. Giggles after found, never before.
  4. Hold still: once hidden — statue! No peeking, no wiggling. Count five slow breaths.
  5. Play the seek games below and close: "small, quiet, still."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Hide" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly hiding illustration below — exactly as the tucked-in shape looks.

Ask your child

"What three things make a good hide? When are giggles allowed? What does the seeker’s count give us time for?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Small, quiet, still!" "I held still for ten breaths!" or the found joy: "FOUND ME — now I seek!"

Out in the real world

Hides happen in every hallway, garden and furniture gap — and the stillness skill shows up later at picture time, assembly time and library time. Hide-and-seek is regulation practice in a costume.

Try it together

Hide-and-Seek Classic: seeker counts to ten at the wall (loud, proud counting gives hiders their runway), hiders get small-quiet-still, the seek begins. Rule for hiders: still until FOUND — being found means a big "FOUND!" shout and a giggle release. Swap every round so everyone seeks once. Ten breaths of stillness per hide: the best self-control gym in childhood.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three hide skills. When do the giggles come out? What is being found called?" Small-quiet-still, after found, FOUND — three answers and the seek is on.

Parent tips

Give the seeker a real counting voice — the hiders need the runway. And let the youngest hide FIRST and nearest: early success builds the stillness appetite.

This lesson pairs with the Hide flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Jump — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches jumping in its four honest beats — bend the knees, swing the arms, fly on two feet, land soft as a frog — the pattern every puddle, line and podium jump shares.

What is this?

Jump is leaving the ground with both feet and landing again: knees bend to load, arms swing to lift, the body flies, and the landing bends the knees again to catch the fall softly.

What does it mean?

The jump’s secret is that landing is half the skill: a jump that ends stiff is a stomp that hurts. Bend-swing-fly-BEND gives children the whole arc — and soft landings are the habit that keeps jumping joyful for years.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three jump ideas: the knees are springs — they bend BEFORE the jump to load and AFTER to land; the arms swing UP with the jump — free lift from the wings; and two feet leave together, frog-style.

Why this matters

Jumping is the wall’s most-repeated power move — hops, skips, vaults and dance all borrow its bend-swing-land — and soft landings protect every joint that will ever leap.

What it teaches

Two-foot take-off and landing, arm-leg coordination, force loading (the pre-bend), and the frog-soft landing that makes repetition safe.

Words to learn

jumpbendswingtwo feetlandsoftfrog

Say this to your child

“"Jumping has four beats! BEND the knees — load the springs. SWING the arms up — wings give free lift. FLY on two feet — frog on a lily pad! And land BENT — soft as a frog, quiet as a leaf. Bend, swing, fly, land: every puddle-jump in the world uses the same four beats!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is jump — bend, swing, fly, land soft!"
  2. The springs: bend the knees — feel the spring load. Jump straight up and BEND on landing — boing! The bend catches you.
  3. The wings: arms swing UP as the feet leave — try a jump with arms glued down (small!), then with the swing (big!). The arms are free lift.
  4. The frog landing: land on two feet, knees bent, like a frog on a lily pad — silent as a frog is the goal.
  5. Play the jump games below and close: "bend, swing, frog-land."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Jump" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly jumping illustration below — exactly as the airborne frog pose looks.

Ask your child

"When do the knees bend — twice or never? What do the arms do? What lands quietly?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Bend, swing, fly, land!" "My arms gave me free lift!" or the frog report: "Frog-landing — silent as a leaf!"

Out in the real world

Puddle-jumps, chalk lines, the last stair-hope — jumps wait everywhere. The four beats transfer to every one, and the frog-landing is the habit that keeps them all painless.

Try it together

Puddle Line: chalk puddles on the ground — small, middle, wide. Jump each with the four beats: bend… swing… fly… frog-land. Score the landings by SOUND: a quiet frog-land earns a croak of approval, a stompy land earns "again — softer!" Then the lily-pad course: five puddles in a row, frog-hopped with springs and wings. Bend, swing, fly, land — the puddle line is a gym.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the four beats. What lifts for free? How does a frog land?" Bend-swing-fly-land, the arms, soft and bent — three answers and the puddles are jumped.

Parent tips

"Land like a frog" works better than "land softly" — the animal picture does the coaching. And hold the arms-glued comparison once: feeling the free lift sells the swing forever.

This lesson pairs with the Jump flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Kick — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the kick’s two-part secret: the plant foot beside the ball, and the swing from the hip — taught in slow motion before the ball ever flies.

What is this?

Kick is striking a ball with the foot: the standing foot plants beside the ball, the kicking leg swings from the hip with the toe down, and the ball leaves fast and true.

What does it mean?

The kick is the last ball skill to mature — feet are far from the eyes — so slow-motion teaching matters: the plant foot is where aim lives, and the hip is where power lives. One slow swing teaches both.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three kick ideas: the plant foot stands BESIDE the ball, pointing at the target — the aim is in the plant; the swing comes from the HIP, the whole leg like a pendulum; and the toe points DOWN at contact — the top of the foot is the striker.

Why this matters

Kicking is the first sport skill most children love — and a clean plant-and-swing at two or three becomes the soccer strike at five without relearning.

What it teaches

Single-leg balance on the plant (a hidden skill!), hip-swing power, aiming with body position, and the follow-through that keeps the kick honest.

Words to learn

kickplant footswinghiptoe downtargetswing

Say this to your child

“"Kicking has two secrets! The plant foot stands BESIDE the ball, pointing where you want the ball to go — your aim lives in your standing foot. And the kick leg swings from the HIP, big like a pendulum, toe pointing down. Slow motion first — plant… swing… whack! — then let it fly!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is kick — one foot plants, one foot swings."
  2. The plant: stand beside the ball, plant foot pointing at the target — "your standing foot is the aim." Try it: point the plant, see where the ball will go.
  3. The swing: the kicking leg swings from the HIP, big and slow in slow motion — a pendulum, toe down.
  4. Slow-motion kick: the whole kick at quarter speed — plant… swing… contact… follow through. Three slow ones before one real one.
  5. Play the kick games below and close: "plant beside, swing from the hip."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Kick" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly kicking illustration below — exactly as the swing and ball look.

Ask your child

"Where does the plant foot stand? Where does the swing start — knee or hip? Which way does the toe point?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Plant beside, aim with my foot!" "Swing from the hip — pendulum!" or the striker: "Toe down — whack!"

Out in the real world

Kicks wait in every garden ball, hallway soft-ball and playground pitch — and the plant-foot aim transfers to every one. Slow-motion first is how soccer schools teach it too.

Try it together

Slow-Motion League: three quarter-speed kicks before every real one — plant… swing… contact — then the real kick at a two-chair goal. Then the target round: a chalk X on the fence or wall — plant foot aimed at the X, ball flies, X hit earns a roar. Five kicks each, plant-aimed every time. The aim lives in the plant — the slow league proves it.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where is the aim? Where does the swing start? Which way does the toe point?" The plant foot, the hip, down — three answers and the ball flies true.

Parent tips

A size-1 mini ball or soft toy ball makes early contact easy and honest. And the slow-motion rule is the lesson: children who can KICK SLOWLY own the pattern for real.

This lesson pairs with the Kick flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Play — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the word that names the whole place: PLAY — and the three quiet rules that make play good: fair turns, real rules, all-in hearts.

What is this?

Play is games done for joy: chasing, building, pretending, ball games — alone or together. Good play has everyone joining, rules that hold and fun that does not need a winner.

What does it mean?

Play is childhood’s work and the playground’s constitution: turns are shared, rules are kept, and the kid who plays ALL IN makes every game better. Teaching play-as-a-skill makes the whole playground friendlier.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three play ideas: turns are the tax every game pays — everyone gets one; rules are what make it a GAME — changed mid-game, they break it; and all-in is the spirit — half-hearted play is lonely, full-hearted play is contagious.

Why this matters

Play is the container for every other card on this wall — and naming its rules early (turns, rules, all-in) is the kindest thing a grown-up can do for every game that follows.

What it teaches

Turn-taking, rule-keeping, inclusive inviting (asking the lonely kid in), and wholehearted participation — the social engine of the playground.

Words to learn

playgameturnrulesfairall ininvite

Say this to your child

“"PLAY is the whole playground in one word! Good play has three rules: everyone gets a TURN — your turn, my turn; the RULES hold — agree first, then play; and everybody plays ALL IN — with your whole heart! And if someone stands alone, play invites them in: ‘Come play with us!’ That is what play means."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is play — the whole playground in one word!"
  2. The turn tax: every game has turns — whose turn is next? Practise saying "your turn, my turn" out loud.
  3. The rule shield: rules make it a game — agree on them BEFORE starting, and the game holds. Change rules mid-game? The game breaks — restart, re-agree.
  4. All-in hearts: half-play is lonely play — jump in with your whole heart, and invite the watcher: "come play!"
  5. Play the make-a-game activity below and close: "turns, rules, all in."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Play" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly playing illustration below — exactly as the happy game looks.

Ask your child

"What does every game pay in? What holds a game together? What do we say to someone standing alone?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Your turn, my turn!" "Rules first, then play!" or the inviter: "Come play with us!"

Out in the real world

Play happens in every yard, class and waiting room — and its three rules are the same everywhere: turns, rules, all-in. The invitation line is the playground’s most powerful sentence.

Try it together

Make-a-Game: the family invents a brand-new game in five minutes — pick a ball, agree two rules ("bounce it twice, then pass"), decide the turns, and PLAY it all-in for ten minutes. Then the invitation drill: one player sits out looking lonely — the players must invite them in with the line. Turns, rules, all-in: a game made and played by its own constitution.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three rules of good play. What breaks a game mid-way? What invites a watcher in?" Turns-rules-all-in, changed rules, "come play" — three answers and the playground is kind.

Parent tips

Two rules maximum for home-made games — playable beats clever. And rehearse the invitation line until it is automatic: it is the skill that fills empty playground minutes.

This lesson pairs with the Play flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Pull — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches pulling — force that comes TOWARD you: knees bent, body leaning back, grip tight — the wagon, the rope, the door, all one pattern.

What is this?

Pull is drawing something toward your body: the wagon handle, the tug-of-war rope, the heavy door. Strong pulling leans the body BACK and lets the legs take the strain.

What does it mean?

Pulling is the mirror twin of pushing — and the posture is its whole secret: pulling with a tall straight body strains the back; pulling with bent knees and a lean-back turns the legs into the engine.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three pull ideas: pull comes TOWARD the body — the target is your own chest; the body leans BACK and the knees BEND — the legs are the engine; and the grip holds tight — thumbs wrapped, knuckles working.

Why this matters

Tug-of-war is the purest strength game in childhood — and its stance (bent, leaning, gripped) is the same one that will safely pull wagons, ropes and doors for life.

What it teaches

Pulling force with leg drive, grip strength, body-lean coordination, and the partnership game — pulling WITH rules (no letting go!).

Words to learn

pullropelean backkneesgriptugtoward

Say this to your child

“"Pulling comes TOWARD you! The secret is the lean-back: knees bent, body leaning away from the rope, and your LEGS walking backward — the legs are the engine, the hands just hold on tight. Thumbs wrapped! Tug-of-war, wagons, heavy doors — every pull is lean-back and leg-power."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is pull — bringing it toward you!"
  2. The lean-back: hold hands with a partner and pull — feel how leaning BACK makes you strong? Tall-and-forward is weak; bent-and-back is the engine.
  3. The grip: thumbs wrapped around the rope — no fingertip holds. Grip like you mean it.
  4. The legs pull: pull a loaded laundry basket (the wagon) — knees bent, lean back, LEGS walk backward. The legs are the muscle.
  5. Play the tug games below and close: "lean back, legs pull, grip tight."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Pull" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly pulling illustration below — exactly as the lean-back looks.

Ask your child

"Which way does a pull go — away or toward? Where does the engine live — arms or legs? What do the thumbs do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Lean back — pull toward me!" "My legs are the engine!" or the grip check: "Thumbs wrapped, rope won’t slip!"

Out in the real world

Pulls wait in every wagon handle, garden gate and pet lead — and the lean-back stance transfers to all of them. Even getting dressed pulls: sleeves toward the body, lean back, legs strong.

Try it together

Tug-of-War Rules: a soft rope or towel, feet planted, knees bent, lean back — pull the marker (a ribbon on the rope) across your line. Rules: never LET GO (the fall rule), stop on the call, lean back not down. Then the wagon pull: load a laundry basket with two toys, pull it across the room — lean-back legs, tight grip. Two pulls, one stance, real strength.

Understanding check

Ask: "Toward or away? What is the engine? What do the thumbs do?" Toward, the legs, wrap — three answers and the pull is strong.

Parent tips

Never-let-go is the safety spine of every tug game — say it before, during, after. And softer is better early: a towel rope teaches the stance without rope burns.

This lesson pairs with the Pull flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Push — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches pushing — force that goes AWAY from you: hands flat, knees bent, and the power arriving from the legs, not the shoulders.

What is this?

Push is sending something away from the body: the swing start, the box across the floor, the door opening, the merry-go-round — flat hands, bent knees, steady force.

What does it mean?

Pushing is the wall’s every-day strength move, and its secret is the same as pulling’s mirror: the legs supply the force, the arms just aim it. And gentle steady pushes beat wild shoves — especially on swings and little brothers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three push ideas: push travels AWAY — from the chest or the hands, out into the world; the knees bend so the LEGS can help — straight-arm shoulder-shoving is weak and wobbly; and steady beats wild — three gentle pushes move more than one smash.

Why this matters

Pushing starts every swing ride and merry-go-round, opens every heavy door — and the steady-push habit is also the gentle-hands lesson for smaller siblings.

What it teaches

Pushing force with leg drive, force control (gentle to strong), hand placement (flat, spread), and the swing-timing introduction.

Words to learn

pushawayflat handskneessteadygentleswing

Say this to your child

“"Pushing goes AWAY from you! Flat hands, fingers spread — a steady platform. And bend your knees: the legs are the engine, the arms just aim. Steady beats wild — three gentle pushes make a swing soar where one smash barely moves it. Push away, push steady, push strong!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is push — sending it away from you!"
  2. The flat hands: palms flat, fingers spread on the target — a steady platform, not fingers poking.
  3. The legs help: push a box with straight legs (weak!), then with bent knees (strong!). The legs are the engine here too.
  4. Steady beats wild: one smash moves a swing once; three steady pushes make it soar. Practise the gentle-push rhythm.
  5. Play the push games below and close: "flat hands, bent knees, steady."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Push" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly pushing illustration below — exactly as the flat hands look.

Ask your child

"Which way does a push go? Where is the engine? What wins — one smash or three steady pushes?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Away from me!" "Legs help — bent knees!" or the swing-starter: "Three steady pushes — look how high!"

Out in the real world

Pushes open every heavy door, start every swing, load every shopping trolley — and the bent-knee stance transfers to all of them. The gentle-push rhythm is also the little-brother treaty.

Try it together

Swing Starts: at the playground swing or a rope swing at home — three steady pushes from behind, hands flat, knees bent, watching the swing’s rhythm. Count together: push… two, three… push! Then the box relay: push a loaded box around a chair-slalom — steady pushes only, wild ones restart the course. Flat hands, bent knees, steady: the pusher’s whole craft.

Understanding check

Ask: "Away or toward? What is the engine? What wins the swing?" Away, the legs, steady — three answers and the push is smooth.

Parent tips

Watch-the-rhythm is the swing lesson — push WITH the swing, never against. And the wild-push restart rule keeps the box relay honest and hilarious.
