PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Run — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches running as a whole-body team: arms pump with the legs, feet land light, eyes look ahead — and stopping on the word is part of the sport.

What is this?

Run is fast travel on foot: arms bent and pumping opposite the legs, feet landing light and quick, eyes ahead — and a good runner can STOP when the word comes.

What does it mean?

Children run for joy before they run for sport — the teaching gift is the teamwork story (arms help legs!) and the stop-skill: a runner who can stop on command is safe on every playground and street.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three run ideas: the arms PUMP, bent at the elbows, opposite to the legs — pumping arms lift the run; light feet — quiet quick steps, not thunder stomps; and the stop is trained — one word, feet plant, body brakes.

Why this matters

Running is the wall’s most-used skill — every chase, every race, every game of tag — and arm-pump plus stop-on-word turns joyful chaos into actual sport.

What it teaches

Arm-leg opposition (a real coordination milestone), light-landing gait, stopping control, and the joy of open sprinting.

Words to learn

runarms pumplight feetsprintstopfinish linefast

Say this to your child

“"Running is arms-and-legs teamwork! Pump your arms, bent elbows, opposite to your legs — feel the lift? Land light like a quiet fox — quick steps, no thunder. And a good runner can STOP: one word, feet plant, statue! Arms pump, feet light, stop on the word — now race me to the tree!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is run — fast feet and pumping arms!"
  2. The arms: elbows bent, fists soft, pump them opposite the legs — walk slowly while pumping to feel the teamwork.
  3. The light feet: run like a quiet fox — quick light steps. Thunder-stomps slow you down; light feet fly.
  4. The stop: practise "run… STOP!" — feet plant, body brakes, statue. Three stops without toppling wins the badge.
  5. Play the run games below and close: "arms pump, feet light, stop on the word."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Run" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly running illustration below — exactly as the pumping arms look.

Ask your child

"What do the arms do? What do quiet fox feet sound like? What happens on the word STOP?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Arms pump opposite!" "Light feet — quiet fox!" or the braked one: "STOP — statue, no topple!"

Out in the real world

Runs fill every playground, garden and hallway (carefully!) — and the arm-pump is visible on every sprinter on screen: watch a race and find the teamwork. The stop skill is the street-crossing skill too.

Try it together

Line Races + Stop Badge: two chalk lines, sprint between them with pumping arms and light feet — race after race, joy first. Then the Stop Badge round: run freely until the call — "STOP!" — plant and statue; three clean stops earn the stop badge (any sticker). Finish with a lap of honour, arms pumping. Fast feet, fox steps, trustworthy brakes.

Understanding check

Ask: "What pumps opposite the legs? What do light feet sound like? What is the stop skill for?" The arms, a quiet fox, safety — three answers and the race is on.

Parent tips

Walk-and-pump first for the arm-leg opposition — slow motion teaches the pattern. And never call STOP mid-stride of the youngest runner: call it on the landing beat.

This lesson pairs with the Run flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Sit — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches sitting down as a real skill: criss-cross legs, hands resting, body calm — the superpower that runs story time, circle time and every classroom after.

What is this?

Sit is coming to rest on the ground or a seat: cross the legs (criss-cross!), rest the hands, settle the body — sitting still is listening with your whole posture.

What does it mean?

Between the running and the climbing sits the sit — the skill that lets a child JOIN story time, assembly and every group moment. Framed as a skill (not a command), sitting calm becomes something children can practise and own.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sit ideas: criss-cross legs make a steady base — a basket the body sits in; hands REST — in the lap, on the knees, holding a book; and calm is the game — still body, soft face, ears open.

Why this matters

Group sitting is the gateway to every classroom skill for the next twelve years — taught here as a game on the grass, where it first belongs.

What it teaches

Postural control, stillness stamina (built in seconds, not demands), group calm, and the transition skill — running to sitting to running.

Words to learn

sitcriss-crosscalmstilllapstory timesettle

Say this to your child

“"Sitting down is a real skill! Cross your legs — criss-cross — and sit in the basket: steady base, tall back. Hands REST in your lap. Then the settle: three slow breaths, shoulders down — calm as a pond. Sitting calm lets you join every story, every circle, every song. Criss-cross… settle… listen!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is sit — the calm-down skill!"
  2. The basket: cross the legs — criss-cross — and sit INSIDE the basket: steady base, tall back.
  3. The resting hands: hands go to the lap or the knees — resting, not fidgeting. Try both; pick a home for the hands.
  4. The settle: three slow breaths, shoulders down, soft face — sitting calm is a game you can win.
  5. Play the sitting games below and close: "criss-cross, hands rest, settle."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Sit" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly sitting illustration below — exactly as the criss-cross calm looks.

Ask your child

"What does criss-cross make — a basket or a puddle? Where do the hands rest? How many breaths in the settle?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Criss-cross basket!" "Hands rest in my lap!" or the settled one: "Three breaths — calm as a pond!"

Out in the real world

Sitting moments fill every day: story time, meal time, bus seats, the cinema — and the criss-cross basket transfers to all of them. The settle is also the bedtime trick.

Try it together

Circle-Time Practice: everyone sits criss-cross in a circle — the settle, three breaths. Then story time for ONE minute (a very short story!) with statue-calm: still body, hands resting. Break, run a lap, sit again — the run-to-sit transition is the real skill. Three rounds, story a little longer each time. Criss-cross, hands rest, settle: the classroom superpower, grown on grass.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does criss-cross make? Where do the hands go? What is the settle?" A basket, the lap, three breaths — three answers and the circle is calm.

Parent tips

Seconds matter: ten calm seconds is a win at two, a minute is a triumph at four — grow slowly. And let the run-lap between sits be joyous: the transition is half the skill.

This lesson pairs with the Sit flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Slide — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the slide’s two golden rules — feet first, one at a time — and the whoosh that makes the waiting worth it.

What is this?

Slide is the playground’s gift ride: climb up, sit at the top, feet first down the slope, land at the bottom, clear away — and the turn-taking is part of the ride.

What does it mean?

The slide is where the playground’s social rules meet its physics: feet first (gravity’s rule), one at a time (everyone’s rule), clear away (the next rider’s rule). Three rules, total harmony, maximum whoosh.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three slide ideas: feet FIRST, always — sitting up or headfirst is the one no; one rider at a time — the slide is a queue, and the queue is fair; and clear away at the bottom — the next whoosh is waiting behind you.

Why this matters

The slide teaches turn-taking at its most tempting moment — when waiting is hardest — which is exactly why it works: the whoosh rewards the queue.

What it teaches

Turn-taking under excitement, body positioning (feet-first sitting), the clear-away habit, and the climb-slide-repeat rhythm that builds patience plus courage.

Words to learn

slidefeet firstturnwaitwhooshclear awayqueue

Say this to your child

“"The slide has two golden rules and one big whoosh! Feet FIRST down the slope — your feet are the brakes, so they go first. ONE rider at a time — wait your turn in the queue, it is fair for everybody. Land, stand, clear away — the next whoosh is waiting! Climb… sit… whoosh… again!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is slide — the whoosh machine!"
  2. Rule one: feet FIRST — sit at the top, feet point down the slope, hands holding the sides. Never headfirst — the feet are the brakes.
  3. Rule two: ONE at a time — wait until the rider before has landed and cleared. The queue is fair for everybody.
  4. Rule three: clear away — land, stand up, step aside: the next whoosh is waiting.
  5. Play the slide rhythm below and close: "feet first, one at a time, clear away."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Slide" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly sliding illustration below — exactly as the feet-first whoosh looks.

Ask your child

"What goes first — feet or head? How many riders at once? What do we do at the bottom?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Feet first — the brakes!" "One at a time, then me!" or the whoosh report: "Cleared away — next rider, go!"

Out in the real world

Slides wait in every playground — and the three rules travel to every one of them, whatever their height. The clear-away habit even works at the top of stairs.

Try it together

Slide Queue Rhythm: at the slide, practise the full rhythm out loud — climb up, sit top, FEET FIRST, whoosh, land, clear away, "next!" — three rounds each with counting turns. Then the queue game: the waiters count the whooshes aloud while waiting — the counting turns waiting into watching. Feet first, one at a time, clear away: the fairest machine on the playground.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes first? How many riders? What happens after landing?" Feet, one, clear away — three answers and the whoosh is fair.

Parent tips

Say the rules at the BOTTOM of the ladder, not the top — rules announced calmly stick better than rules shouted mid-climb. And honour the queue: the counting waiters are practising exactly the patience the slide exists to teach.

This lesson pairs with the Slide flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Swing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the swing’s real mechanics: hands hold, seat stays, legs PUMP — forward out, back in — plus the mount and dismount that keep the whole ride safe.

What is this?

Swing is riding a hanging seat: hold the chains or ropes tight, keep the seat under you, and PUMP the legs — out on the way forward, tucked on the way back — until the sky swings by.

What does it mean?

The swing is the playground’s physics teacher: legs pump in rhythm WITH the swing (not against it), the timing is the engine, and holding on is the non-negotiable. The dismount — slowing, stopping, stepping off — is the trained ending every ride needs.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three swing ideas: hands HOLD and the seat stays under you — standing or jumping off is the one no; legs PUMP — stretch out forward, tuck back — in rhythm with the swing; and the dismount is trained: slow… stop… step off — never leap from the sky.

Why this matters

Pump timing is a genuine rhythm skill (the swing’s clock, like the beat!), and the mount-dismount routine is the safety habit that keeps flying joyful for years.

What it teaches

Rhythmic leg pumping, timing-to-a-moving-system, grip endurance, and the controlled dismount — patience at the end of the fun.

Words to learn

swingpumpholdseatrhythmslowdismount

Say this to your child

“"Swinging is legs pumping the sky! Hands hold the chains, seat stays under you — all the way. Legs PUMP: stretch out as you fly forward, tuck in as you swing back — out… in… out… in — with the swing’s own rhythm. And when the ride is done: slow… stop… step off. Never leap from the sky — the ground is not going anywhere!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is swing — legs pump the sky!"
  2. The hold: both hands grip the chains, seat firmly under you — "hands and seat stay all the way." Standing up or jumping off is the one no.
  3. The pump: legs stretch OUT as you swing forward, tuck UNDER as you swing back — out… in… out… in — in rhythm with the swing.
  4. The dismount: when the ride ends — slow swings first, then stop, then STEP off. Never leap from the sky.
  5. Play the pump games below and close: "hands hold, legs pump, step off."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Swing" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly swinging illustration below — exactly as the pumping legs look.

Ask your child

"What holds and what pumps? When do the legs stretch out? How do we end the ride?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hands hold, legs pump!" "Out when forward, tuck when back!" or the safe ender: "Slow… stop… step off!"

Out in the real world

Swings hang in every playground — and the pump rhythm is the same on every one: with the swing, never against. The step-off habit is the transfer skill for every ride, ladder and climbing frame after.

Try it together

Pump-Rhythm School: on the swing, grown-up starts the gentle motion. Legs practise the pump — out… in… out… in — spoken out loud until the rhythm catches the swing’s clock. Ride till the sky ticks by, then the dismount routine: wait for slow… stop… step off, both feet. Three rides, three clean dismounts, one badge. Hands hold, legs pump, the sky pumps back.

Understanding check

Ask: "What stays and what pumps? When do the legs tuck? How does the ride end?" Hands and seat, on the back-swing, slow-stop-step — three answers and the sky pumps too.

Parent tips

Say the pump out loud — the words synchronise the legs to the swing faster than any demonstration. And end every ride with the routine, every time: the trained ending is the safety net.

This lesson pairs with the Swing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Walk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches walking as the skill it is: heel to toe, eyes ahead, walking feet where walking feet belong — the calm travel that runs the whole day.

What is this?

Walk is steady travel on foot: heel lands first, then the toe rolls, eyes ahead, arms swinging easy — and in walk-zones (car parks, corridors, pool-sides) walking feet are the rule.

What does it mean?

Walking is the underrated skill between crawling and running — the heel-toe roll makes it smooth, the eyes-ahead make it safe, and the walk-zone idea gives it a social job: some places are for walking feet.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three walk ideas: heel first, toe rolls — smooth steps, not flat stamps; eyes AHEAD — the walk steers by looking forward; and walk-zones exist — car parks, corridors and pool-sides belong to walking feet.

Why this matters

Walking is the day’s background skill — done well it is safe, smooth and unremarkable, which is exactly the point: a good walker saves all their drama for the playground.

What it teaches

Heel-toe gait pattern, eyes-ahead steering, zone awareness (walk vs run places), and calm-paced travel as self-regulation.

Words to learn

walkheeltoerollaheadwalk-zonesteady

Say this to your child

“"Walking is heel… toe… roll! Heel lands first, toe rolls after — smooth steps, not flat stamps. Eyes AHEAD — your eyes steer your walk. And some places are walk-zones: the car park, the corridor, the pool-side — walking feet only there! Running feet wait for the grass. Heel, toe, eyes ahead: steady as you go."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is walk — heel to toe, eyes ahead!"
  2. The roll: heel lands first, toe rolls after — heel… toe… heel… toe. Try it slow-motion, then smooth.
  3. The steering: eyes look ahead, not at the feet — "your eyes steer your walk," same as the balance lesson.
  4. The zones: name the walk-zones — car park, corridor, pool-side: "walking feet here!" Running feet wait for the grass.
  5. Play the walk games below and close: "heel, toe, eyes ahead."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Walk" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly walking illustration below — exactly as the heel-toe step looks.

Ask your child

"What lands first — heel or toe? What steers the walk? Name a walk-zone."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Heel… toe… roll!" "My eyes steer!" or the zone-keeper: "Walking feet in the car park!"

Out in the real world

Walks fill every day — to the car, along the shop aisle, down the school corridor — and the heel-toe roll plus eyes-ahead makes each one smooth. The walk-zone idea is the car-park rule that matters most.

Try it together

Walk-Line Parade: chalk line or kerb — walk it heel-toe, eyes on the end target, arms swinging easy. Then the zone game: tape a "car park" zone and a "grass" zone — walking feet in the park, running feet allowed on the grass, and the switch on the line is the game. Steady steps, sharp zones: the walker’s licence, earned today.

Understanding check

Ask: "What rolls after the heel? What steers the walk? Where do running feet wait?" The toe, the eyes, the grass — three answers and the walk is smooth.

Parent tips

Slow-motion heel-toe first — the roll disappears at speed unless it was learned slow. And the zone switch is the fun: run FREE on the grass, walk PROUD in the park.

This lesson pairs with the Walk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ball — the playground’s most willing toy — and its three tricks: roll it, bounce it, throw it. One ball, a hundred games, all starting here.

What is this?

A ball is a round toy that rolls, bounces and flies: the round shape means it always moves, and every game on the playground — catch, kick, bowling, tag-with-a-ball — runs on one.

What does it mean?

The ball is the best first sports tool because it is honest: it goes exactly where the force sends it. Roll it gently and it rolls gently — the ball is a force teacher, and every push and throw is a lesson it answers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ball ideas: ROLLING is the floor trick — push from underneath, along the ground; BOUNCING is the push-down trick — the ball comes back for more; and gentle hands — the ball is a friend, and friends are not thrown at faces.

Why this matters

Every ball game the child will ever play — soccer, basketball, tennis — is one of these three tricks grown up. Learn the ball’s three tricks and the whole world of sport opens.

What it teaches

Force control (gentle to strong), tracking a moving ball, the three-strike vocabulary (roll-bounce-throw), and the gentle-hands social rule.

Words to learn

ballrollbouncethrowroundgentlegame

Say this to your child

“"The ball is the playground’s most willing toy — it knows three tricks! ROLL it — push from underneath along the floor. BOUNCE it — push down, and it comes back for more! THROW it — underarm, gentle, to a friend’s chest. One ball, three tricks, a hundred games. And the ball rule: gentle hands — the ball is a friend!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is ball — the playground’s most willing toy!"
  2. Trick one, roll: push from UNDERNEATH, along the floor — rolling is the floor trick. Roll it to a partner and back.
  3. Trick two, bounce: push DOWN from above — the ball comes back up! Catch it. Bouncing is the push-down trick.
  4. Trick three, throw: underarm toss to a partner’s chest — the flying trick, taught gentle.
  5. Play the follow-the-ball game below and close: "roll, bounce, throw — gentle hands."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Ball" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly ball illustration below — exactly as the round toy looks.

Ask your child

"Name the ball’s three tricks. Which trick pushes from underneath? What is the ball rule for friends?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Roll, bounce, throw!" "Bounce — it comes back for more!" or the gentle one: "Gentle hands — the ball is a friend!"

Out in the real world

Balls live in every home, park and school bag — and the three tricks are the first three skills of every sport. Roll one tonight down the hallway: the willingness is contagious.

Try it together

Follow-the-Ball: one ball, all three tricks in a circuit — roll to your partner, partner bounces three times and catches, partner throws back underarm. Run the circuit five times, then swap order. Finish with trick-invention: what ELSE can the ball do? (Spin it, balance it on the head, roll it down the slide-approach!) The willing toy rewards every idea.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three tricks. Which comes back by itself? What is the friend rule?" Roll-bounce-throw, the bounce, gentle hands — three answers and the games begin.

Parent tips

Start with a mid-size soft ball — big enough to track, soft enough to fail. And the gentle-hands rule is said every round: it is the treaty that keeps every future ball game kind.

This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Bench — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the bench — the playground’s quiet wooden plank with three jobs: a seat for resting, a beam for balancing, and a stage for pretending.

What is this?

A bench is a long wooden or metal seat: built for resting, but the playground’s best improvisers use it as a balance beam, a shop counter, a pirate ship rail, a stage.

What does it mean?

The bench teaches the playground’s deepest idea: equipment is what you MAKE of it. The same plank that rests the tired legs walks the tightrope for the brave ones — imagination is the only upgrade it needs.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bench ideas: the bench is a RESTING spot — tired bodies sit, breathe and watch; it is a BALANCE beam — walk it slow, wings out (from the balance lesson); and it is a STAGE — up top for shows, but jump down with bent knees.

Why this matters

Open-ended play — one object, many uses — is the creative core of playground culture, and the bench is its friendliest example: every child can rest on it, walk it or crown themselves on it.

What it teaches

Imaginative transformation (one object, many jobs), balance-beam walking, rest-spot self-regulation (knowing when to sit), and safe dismounts.

Words to learn

benchseatbeamstagerestwalk the plankpretend

Say this to your child

“"The bench is one wooden plank with three jobs! Tired? It is a SEAT — sit, breathe, watch. Brave? It is a BALANCE BEAM — wings out, walk it slow. Imaginative? It is a STAGE — up top, ‘welcome to the show!’ — and jump down with bent knees, frog-style. One bench, three jobs, your choice!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a bench — a seat with three jobs!"
  2. Job one, rest: tired legs sit here — breathe, watch the playground, rejoin when refuelled. Resting is playing too.
  3. Job two, beam: walk the bench edge slow — wings out, eyes ahead — the bench is the beginner’s tightrope.
  4. Job three, stage: stand UP TOP and announce — "welcome to the show!" Then dismount with bent knees: jump down like a frog, not a statue.
  5. Play the bench games below and close: "rest, beam, stage."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Bench" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly bench illustration below — exactly as the wooden plank looks.

Ask your child

"Name the bench’s three jobs. How do we walk the beam? How do we come down from the stage?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Seat, beam, stage!" "Wings out — walking the plank!" or the show-off: "Welcome to the show — frog-dismount!"

Out in the real world

Benches line every park, bus stop and garden — and the three jobs travel with them: rest on the bus-stop bench, beam on the garden edge, stage on the picnic table. Imagination included free.

Try it together

Bench Three-Jobs Circuit: rest thirty seconds (breathe, watch), then walk the beam slow with wings out, then the stage: announce a tiny show — a joke, a bow, a song line — and frog-dismount. Three rounds, rotating who announces. One plank, all three jobs, the whole playground in miniature.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three jobs. What walks the beam? What dismounts the stage?" Seat-beam-stage, wings out, bent knees — three answers and the bench performs.

Parent tips

Beam before stage: balance earns the height. And the frog-dismount rule is stated every stage round — bent knees catch what straight legs jolt.

This lesson pairs with the Bench flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Climbing Frame — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the climbing frame — the playground’s mountain — crossed with the three-point rule, a planned route, and the proud descent.

What is this?

A climbing frame is a structure of bars, rungs and platforms built for going up, across and down: ladders, nets and poles joined into one mountain of possibilities.

What does it mean?

The frame is where the action lessons meet: climbing’s three-point rule, balance’s steady beams, the planned route — it is a whole curriculum in steel. And the route-plan is the thinking skill: eyes climb first, body follows.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three frame ideas: the three-point rule runs every crossing — three touch, one moves; plan the route BEFORE climbing — eyes climb first; and space your riders — one body per bar-section, no stacking.

Why this matters

Frame play grows real bravery: height, planning and the proud down-climb. A child who plans a route and completes it has done architecture, athletics and courage in one go.

What it teaches

Route planning (visual-motor sequencing), three-point crossing, spacing awareness (others on the frame), and the proud planned descent.

Words to learn

climbing framerouteplanthree pointscrossplatformdown

Say this to your child

“"The climbing frame is the playground’s mountain — and mountains are crossed with a PLAN! Eyes climb first: name your route — ladder, across, down. Then the three-point rule all the way: three points touch, one moves. One rider per section — the frame is big enough when nobody rushes. Plan it, cross it, and come down PROUD!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the climbing frame — the playground’s mountain!"
  2. Eyes climb first: look the route over — which ladder, which bar, which platform? Say it out loud: "ladder, across, slide down." Plan before hands.
  3. Three points, always: on any crossing — three touch, one moves. Count it like the ladder lesson.
  4. Space the riders: one body per section — if someone is on the bridge, wait at the platform. The frame is big enough when nobody rushes.
  5. Play the route games below and close: "plan, cross, proud down."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Climbing Frame" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly frame illustration below — exactly as the mountain of bars looks.

Ask your child

"What climbs first — eyes or hands? How many points touch? How many bodies per bar-section?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Eyes climb first — I named my route!" "Three points, one move!" or the spacer: "I waited at the platform — the bridge was busy!"

Out in the real world

Climbing frames stand in every park and school yard — and the route-plan habit transfers to every new one: eyes first, always. The proud down-climb is the courage certificate.

Try it together

Route-Naming Club: at the frame, each climber NAMES their route aloud — "ladder up, bar-bridge across, pole down" — then climbs it with the three-point count. Then the new-route round: invent a DIFFERENT way across than last time. Finish with the proud descent: down slow, feet landing on purpose, arms up at the bottom: "I planned it, I crossed it!" The mountain respects planners.

Understanding check

Ask: "What climbs first? What is the crossing rule? What does a proud climber do at the bottom?" The eyes, three-points, arms up — three answers and the mountain is crossed.

Parent tips

Name-routes-before-hands every single time — the spoken plan is the safety plan. And celebrate the WAITING at platforms as much as the crossing: spacing is frame-manners.

This lesson pairs with the Climbing Frame flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Fence — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fence — the playground’s border that says: inside here, everything is yours; the fence is not a wall against fun, it is the fun’s own edge.

What is this?

A fence is the border around the playground: bars or panels that mark where the play world ends. It keeps riders, runners and roamers inside the safe zone — and the gate is its one polite door.

What does it mean?

The fence teaches boundaries as kindness: inside the fence, every game is allowed; the edge is where children check in with their grown-up. Freedom feels bigger, not smaller, when its edge is known.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fence ideas: the fence marks the play world — inside is yours, explore it all; the edge is a CHECK-IN spot — back to the fence means back to the grown-up’s eyes; and the gate is the one door — opened and closed by grown-ups, never the escape hatch.

Why this matters

Boundary awareness is the safety skill under all free play — a child who knows the edge plays braver INSIDE it, and the check-in habit is the reunification skill every crowded place needs.

What it teaches

Boundary awareness, check-in habit-building, gate manners, and the secure-base idea — edges make exploration brave.

Words to learn

fenceborderedgeinsidegatecheck-inboundary

Say this to your child

“"The fence is the playground’s border — and inside it, everything is YOURS! The swings, the sand, the whole play world. The fence’s one job is the edge: when you reach it, look back and WAVE — a check-in with your grown-up. And the gate is the one polite door — it belongs to the grown-ups. Free inside, waving at the edge: that is how the playground stays kind."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the fence — the playground’s own border."
  2. Inside is yours: the fence marks the play world — every swing, slide and sandbox inside is yours to explore.
  3. The edge check-in: when you reach the fence, look back to your grown-up — a wave is a check-in. Edges are for waving.
  4. The gate rule: the gate is the one door, and it belongs to the grown-ups — players play inside; leaving is a check-in, not a solo mission.
  5. Play the boundary games below and close: "inside is yours, wave at the edge."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Fence" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly fence illustration below — exactly as the border bars look.

Ask your child

"What does the fence mark? What do we do at the edge? Whose door is the gate?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Inside is all mine!" "Wave at the edge — check-in!" or the gate-keeper: "The gate belongs to the grown-ups!"

Out in the real world

Fences border every playground, school yard and pool — and the check-in wave works at every beach, party and supermarket too: edge means eyes-to-grown-up. The bravest explorers know their edges.

Try it together

Edge Check-In Game: at the playground or garden, practise the wave-at-the-edge — run an errand to the fence, turn, wave big, run back. Three check-ins, each greeted with a wave back and a cheer. Then the gate walk: approach the gate TOGETHER, name whose door it is, walk away to play. Inside is yours; the edge is friendly; the game is freedom with a wave.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the fence mark? What happens at the edge? Whose is the gate?" The play world, a wave check-in, the grown-ups’ — three answers and the freedom is safe.

Parent tips

Greet every check-in wave warmly — a dull response trains fewer waves. And name the fence’s job as kindness, not restriction: the edge is why the inside can be wild.

This lesson pairs with the Fence flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ladder — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ladder — the playground’s stairway — climbed to its own rhythm: hand, hand, foot, foot, one rung at a time, all the way to the proud top.

What is this?

A ladder is a row of rungs set in two rails: hands grip the rails or rungs, feet step rung by rung, and the climb is a rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot — repeated to the top.

What does it mean?

The ladder turns climbing into rhythm: the hand-hand-foot-foot beat is a climb you can SAY, and a climb you can say is a climb you can keep safe at any height.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ladder ideas: the rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot — one rung at a time, never skipping; grip the RAILS when resting; and the top rung is a lookout, not a seat — touch it, then plan the down.

Why this matters

The rhythm climb is the safest climb pattern there is — it paces the body, keeps three points touching, and turns a scary height into a counted song.

What it teaches

Rhythmic sequencing, alternating grip-and-step, pace control (the climb’s own speed), and top-of-ladder decision-making.

Words to learn

ladderrungrhythmhandfootgriptop

Say this to your child

“"The ladder climbs to a rhythm — hand, hand, foot, foot! One rung at a time, never skipping, the beat keeps you safe. Rest mid-climb? Grip the rails and breathe. And the top rung is a LOOKOUT, not a seat — touch it, look around, then plan your down-climb. Rung by rung, the whole sky!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a ladder — rung by rung to the top!"
  2. The rhythm: climb saying it — hand… hand… foot… foot — one rung at a time. Never skip a rung; the rhythm is the safety.
  3. The rails rest: pause mid-climb? Hands grip the RAILS, feet planted, breathe. Resting is part of climbing.
  4. The top rung: touch the top — LOOKOUT, not a seat! Look around from the top, then plan the down.
  5. Play the rhythm games below and close: "hand, hand, foot, foot — all the way."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Ladder" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly ladder illustration below — exactly as the rungs look.

Ask your child

"Say the climb rhythm. What do we grip when resting? Is the top rung a seat or a lookout?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hand, hand, foot, foot!" "Rails for resting!" or the lookout: "Top rung — I looked around, then planned my down!"

Out in the real world

Ladders stand in every playground frame, bunk bed and garden — and the rhythm transfers to all of them, including the stairs. A climb you can say is a climb you can keep.

Try it together

Rhythm Climb Counts: on the ladder, climb chanting — hand… hand… foot… foot — slow as a lullaby. Mid-climb rests: grip rails, three breaths, continue. Top-rung lookout: touch, look, name three things you can see from up there, then down-climb the same rhythm. Three climbs, three lookouts, one proud climber. The rhythm is the ladder’s song.

Understanding check

Ask: "Say the rhythm. Where do hands rest? What is the top rung?" Hand-hand-foot-foot, the rails, a lookout — three answers and the ladder is climbed in song.

Parent tips

Chant SLOWLY — the words pace the body; fast chants make fast falls. And the lookout round gives the top a purpose beyond height: looking, then planning down.

This lesson pairs with the Ladder flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Monkey Bars — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the monkey bars — hand over hand across the sky — and its kindest secret: letting go and dropping safely is part of the skill, not a failure of it.

What is this?

Monkey bars are a row of overhead rungs: hands grip, the body hangs, and one hand at a time flies to the next rung — hand over hand, swing and reach, across the sky.

What does it mean?

The bars are the playground’s strength test and its courage test — and the honest rule is that grip gets tired: knowing the safe drop (bend knees, land on feet, roll the landing) is what makes a bar-crosser a bar-PLAYER.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bar ideas: ONE hand flies at a time — the other always holds; the body swings to help reach — a little swing buys the next bar; and the safe drop is trained — bend the knees, let go, land on feet, bend on landing.

Why this matters

Grip strength plus courage plus honest limits — the bars build all three. And the trained drop means no one is ever stuck: the ground is always a safe choice.

What it teaches

Grip strength and endurance, alternating reach (one-hand-fly), body swing for momentum, and the safe drop — the skill that ends every bar session with a landing, not a fall.

Words to learn

monkey barsgriphanghand over handswingreachsafe drop

Say this to your child

“"The monkey bars are hand over hand across the sky! Both hands hang, then ONE hand flies to the next bar — the other always holds. A little swing helps the reach: swing… fly! And the honest secret: grip gets tired — when it says done, the safe drop is trained: bend the knees, let go, land on your feet, bend like a frog. Dropping safe is part of the game!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "These are the monkey bars — hand over hand across the sky!"
  2. The hang: both hands on one bar, body hanging long, feet off the ground — feel the grip. Hang and count to five.
  3. One hand flies: reach ONE hand to the next bar — the other always stays. Hand over hand, the crossing begins.
  4. The swing helps: a small body-swing forward buys the reach — swing… and fly.
  5. Teach the safe drop, then play below: "one hand flies, grip decides, drop lands safe."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Monkey Bars" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly bars illustration below — exactly as the overhead rungs look.

Ask your child

"How many hands fly at a time? What helps the reach? What do we do when the grip says done?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "One hand flies!" "Swing… and reach!" or the honest dropper: "My grip said done — safe drop, frog landing!"

Out in the real world

Monkey bars hang in every serious playground — and the trained drop transfers to every hang: climbing frames, tree branches, pool edges. Grip is honest everywhere; the safe drop honours it.

Try it together

Hang-and-Fly Ladder: hang-and-count (five, then seven, then ten) to build the grip. Then bar-crossings: one bar, then two, then as far as the grip honest says — always one hand flying. Finish every session with the SAFE DROP practice: from the first bar, bend knees, let go, land on feet, frog-bend. Three crossings, three clean drops. The bars respect the honest grip.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many hands fly? What helps the reach? What is the trained ending?" One, the swing, the safe drop — three answers and the sky is crossed.

Parent tips

Practise the drop from LOW first — the skill must exist before the height does. And never tease a drop: the child who drops safely today crosses tomorrow on stronger arms.

This lesson pairs with the Monkey Bars flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Sandbox — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the sandbox — a square of beach in the playground — and its two cultures: shared tools and kind builds, plus the shake-out ritual that ends every visit.

What is this?

A sandbox is a framed pit of sand: dig it, mould it, build in it with buckets and spades — the playground’s construction site, bakery and treasure island all at once.

What does it mean?

The sandbox is the playground’s sharing classroom: tools belong to everybody, builds belong to their makers, and sand thrown is sand that ends nobody’s fun. Its rituals — borrow, return, shake out — are citizenship in miniature.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sandbox ideas: tools are shared — borrow, use, RETURN; builds are respected — the castle is the builder’s, ask before joining or (never) knocking; and the shake-out ritual ends every visit — sand shaken from shoes and pockets stays out of socks, cars and houses.

Why this matters

Sand play builds fine motor, engineering thinking and the sharing rules — and the shake-out ritual is the tidy-up habit every sandbox family needs.

What it teaches

Tool sharing and returning, respect for others’ constructions, sensory building (pour, mould, pat), and the self-care ritual of shaking out.

Words to learn

sandboxbucketspadebuildsharereturnshake out

Say this to your child

“"The sandbox is a square of beach — and it has two golden rules! Tools are SHARED: borrow, use, return. Builds are RESPECTED: the castle belongs to its builder — ask before joining, never knock it down. Build with pat-pat-tip for the perfect cake… and when the visit ends, the SHAKE-OUT: jump and shake the sand from your shoes! Share, build, shake out."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the sandbox — a square of beach!"
  2. The tools treaty: buckets and spades belong to everybody — borrow, use, return them to the tool spot. Returning keeps the pit friendly.
  3. Respect the builds: that castle is the builder’s — ask to join, never knock. Kinds builds make build-friends.
  4. The build craft: fill the bucket, pat it DOWN, tip it slow — the perfect sandcake is pat, pat, tip!
  5. Teach the shake-out, then play below: "share, build, shake out."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Sandbox" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly sandbox illustration below — exactly as the dig-and-build pit looks.

Ask your child

"What do we do with borrowed tools? Whose is the castle? What is the shake-out for?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Borrow, use, return!" "Ask before joining the build!" or the shaker: "Shake-out time — sand stays out of my socks!"

Out in the real world

Sandboxes, beaches and sand tables run on the same two rules — and the shake-out ritual is a beach-day classic: jump, wiggle, shake. The pat-pat-tip cake is engineering’s first lesson.

Try it together

Sandcafe Workshop: build a sand cafe — cakes by pat-pat-tip, roads by spade-draws, a moat by digging. Tools borrowed from the tool spot and RETURNED between uses. Then the neighbour round: a second builder joins — ask, share the space, respect the cakes. Finish with the Shake-Out Song: jump-jump-shake, pockets too! Share, build, shake out: the sandbox’s whole culture, practised.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the tools treaty? Whose is the build? Name the end-of-visit ritual." Borrow-use-return, the builder’s, the shake-out — three answers and the pit is friendly.

Parent tips

Model the return out loud — "spade back to the tool spot!" — the phrase builds the habit. And the shake-out gets a song or a count: rituals with music stick for years.

This lesson pairs with the Sandbox flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Seesaw — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the seesaw — the playground’s two-person machine — and its one big truth: it only works when BOTH riders agree and play gentle.

What is this?

A seesaw is a long board balanced on a middle point: one rider up, one rider down, pushing gently with the legs to tip it back and forth — up, down, up, down, together.

What does it mean?

The seesaw is physics teaching partnership: your lift is their descent — the ride literally cannot happen without the other person. And gentle pushing is the treaty: bounce hard and your partner gets a launch, not a ride.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three seesaw ideas: it takes TWO — the seesaw is the playground’s partnership machine; push GENTLE with the legs — soft bounces, not launches; and when up top, feet ready and hands holding — the ground is close, land soft.

Why this matters

Partner play needs negotiation (ready? set?), empathy (how high is MY partner happy with?) and trust — the seesaw trains all three with a board and a fulcrum.

What it teaches

Partner coordination, force moderation (gentle for the other’s comfort), the ready-set-go ritual, and landing readiness at the top.

Words to learn

seesawpartnergentlebounceupdowntogether

Say this to your child

“"The seesaw is the two-person machine — it needs BOTH of us! You go up when I go down, I go up when you go down. And the treaty is GENTLE: legs push softly, bounces not launches — ‘ready, set, gentle!’ Hands hold at the top, feet ready, land soft. The seesaw only works when both riders play kind."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the seesaw — the two-person machine!"
  2. The partnership: one rider each end — the seesaw needs BOTH to work. Your up is their down!
  3. The gentle treaty: push with the legs, softly — "ready? set? gentle!" Bounces, not launches.
  4. The top position: when you are up — hands hold the handles, feet ready near the ground, land soft when your turn comes down.
  5. Play the partner games below and close: "two riders, gentle bounces, soft landings."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Seesaw" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly seesaw illustration below — exactly as the two riders look.

Ask your child

"How many riders does it need? What is the push treaty? What do hands do at the top?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two riders — your up is my down!" "Ready, set, gentle!" or the kind bouncer: "Soft bounces — my partner is smiling!"

Out in the real world

Seesaws tip in every playground — and the partnership lesson travels to every two-person game: swings pushed for friends, tug-of-war agreed, teeter-totters everywhere. Ready-set-gentle is the universal treaty.

Try it together

Ready-Set-Seesaw: two riders mount, agree the treaty out loud — "ready, set, GENTLE!" — and see-saw with soft leg bounces, partner smiling the whole ride. Then the trade round: bigger rider bounces softer, smaller rider gets the lift — fairness felt in the body. End together: both riders slow it to a stop, dismount, bow to each other. The machine that teaches kindness with a board.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many riders? What is the treaty? What do we do at the top?" Two, gentle, hold and land soft — three answers and the seesaw sings.

Parent tips

The spoken "ready, set, gentle!" is the whole safety system — never start without it. And match riders thoughtfully: a kind big-partner makes the little one’s whole day.

This lesson pairs with the Seesaw flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Playground Slide — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the slide as a machine with three parts — ladder, slope, landing — and the queue system that turns waiting into watching.

What is this?

A slide is a smooth slope with a ladder up and a landing zone down: climb, sit, feet first, and the slope does the rest — gravity is the engine, smoothness is the ride.

What does it mean?

The slide is the playground’s physics lesson: high start, smooth slope, gravity pulls — no pushing needed. And its queue is the fairest system on the playground: first up, first down, clear away.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three slide-machine ideas: three parts — ladder up, slope down, landing out; the slope does the work — sit tall, feet first, no pushing off mid-ride; and the queue is fair — the counting waiters become the slide’s audience.

Why this matters

Understanding the machine (slope + gravity) turns the whoosh from magic into physics a child can name — and the fair queue is the social machinery that runs every ride after.

What it teaches

Machine-part naming, gravity intuition (high to low, smooth is fast), queue patience, and the landing-zone awareness.

Words to learn

slideladderslopegravitylandingqueuewhoosh

Say this to your child

“"The slide is a machine with three parts: the LADDER up, the SLOPE down, the LANDING out! The start is high, the slope is smooth — gravity does the pushing, the whoosh is physics! Sit tall, feet first, ride it out — and the queue is fair: first up, first down, clear the landing. The counting waiters are the audience — every whoosh gets a cheer!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the slide — a machine with three parts!"
  2. The parts: the LADDER up, the SLOPE down, the LANDING out. Name them on any real slide.
  3. The physics: the slope is smooth and the start is high — gravity pulls, the whoosh happens. Sit tall, feet first, let the machine work.
  4. The queue: first up, first down, clear the landing — the counting waiters are the slide’s audience, cheering every whoosh.
  5. Play the machine game below and close: "ladder, slope, landing — and a fair queue."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Slide" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly slide illustration below — exactly as the three-part machine looks.

Ask your child

"Name the slide’s three parts. What does the pushing — you or gravity? What is the queue rule?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ladder, slope, landing!" "Gravity drives the whoosh!" or the queue-keeper: "First up, first down — clear away!"

Out in the real world

Slides stand in every playground — three parts, one engine. And the fair-queue system transfers to every ride and water slide after: the counting waiters make waiting a spectator sport.

Try it together

Machine Tour + Fair Queue: at the slide, name the three parts out loud, then ride the full system — ladder, feet-first, whoosh, land, clear — while the waiters count whooshes and cheer each one. Swap roles until everyone has ridden and everyone has announced. The machine understood, the queue made kind: the slide’s whole physics and politics, in one game.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three parts. What is the engine? What does the audience do?" Ladder-slope-landing, gravity, count and cheer — three answers and the whoosh is physics.

Parent tips

Naming the parts before riding makes the machine familiar — new slides stop being scary when they have the same three names. And the waiter-cheer turns patience into participation.

This lesson pairs with the Playground Slide flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Spring Rider — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the spring rider — the playground’s bouncy steed — and its rhythm: gentle rocks that grow with the spring, hands holding, feet on, and the slow-down for a safe hop off.

What is this?

A spring rider is a shape (horse, rocket, dinosaur) on a big coil spring: sit on, hold the handles, rock back and forth — the spring stores each push and gives it back, bigger.

What does it mean?

The spring rider is the playground’s first pendulum lesson: the spring has its own rhythm, and the ride gets bigger only when the rider pushes WITH the spring’s beat — the swing’s law in miniature.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three spring-rider ideas: hands HOLD the handles, feet rest on the pegs — the hold is the whole ride; push WITH the spring — gentle rocks in the spring’s rhythm grow the ride; and the slow-down ends it: smaller and smaller rocks, then hop off when it is nearly still.

Why this matters

The spring teaches rhythm-with-a-machine safely at ground level — and the slow-down ritual is the trained ending that transfers to swings and every ride after.

What it teaches

Rhythm matching with a spring, gentle force control, grip endurance, and the slow-down dismount — the ending as a skill.

Words to learn

spring riderrockhandlesrhythmgentleslow downhop off

Say this to your child

“"The spring rider is the playground’s bouncy steed! Hands on the handles, feet on the pegs. Rock GENTLY — feel the spring push back — and push WITH its rhythm: the rocks grow bigger all by themselves! And to finish: smaller… smaller… nearly still… hop off. The spring has its own song — ride with it, never against it."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the spring rider — the playground’s bouncy steed!"
  2. The hold: both hands on the handles, feet on the pegs — the hold is the ride’s anchor.
  3. The spring’s rhythm: rock GENTLY at first — feel the spring push back? Push WITH its beat, and the rocks grow bigger on their own.
  4. The slow-down: to finish — make the rocks smaller and smaller… nearly still… and hop off. Never leap from a moving steed.
  5. Play the rock games below and close: "hold, rock with the spring, slow down."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Spring Rider" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly spring-rider illustration below — exactly as the bouncy steed looks.

Ask your child

"What do the hands hold? How do the rocks grow bigger? How does the ride end?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Handles held, feet on pegs!" "I pushed WITH the spring — it grew!" or the slow ender: "Smaller… smaller… hop off!"

Out in the real world

Spring riders graze in every playground — horses, rockets, dinosaurs — and all of them share the spring’s law: push with the rhythm. The slow-down is the swing’s dismount, learned at ground level.

Try it together

Spring Song: mount up, handles held, and rock to the spring’s beat — count the rhythm out loud: rock… rock… rock — feeling the spring join in. Grow the rocks gently, then the slow-down: smaller, smaller, nearly still, hop off with both feet. Three rides, three slow-downs. The steed rewards rhythm-keepers with the biggest, safest ride on the playground.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is held? Whose rhythm grows the ride? How does it end?" The handles, the spring’s, slow-down-hop — three answers and the steed sings.

Parent tips

First rocks are TINY — the spring’s rhythm must be felt before it is pushed. And the slow-down is said out loud every ride: the ending ritual is the transferable skill.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Playground Swing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the swing as a machine with parts — chains, seat, arc — and the safe-ride system that turns the playground’s flying seat into a ritual every rider knows.

What is this?

A swing is a seat hanging from chains or ropes: the seat carries you, the chains hold, and the ride is an arc — up forward, up backward, the sky swinging by on both ends.

What does it mean?

Naming the parts makes the flying seat a known machine: chains hold, seat carries, the arc has two high points and a low middle — and the safe-ride system (mount, hold, pump, slow, step) is the ritual that keeps every flight joyful.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three swing-system ideas: the parts — chains hold, seat carries, the arc flies between two high points; the middle of the arc is the FASTEST part — the ends are the slow, safe corners; and the safe-ride system: mount from the front, hold, pump, slow down, step off.

Why this matters

Known machines feel friendly — naming chains-seat-arc turns the swing’s flight into physics a child can explain, and the five-step system is the ride’s whole safety culture.

What it teaches

Machine-part naming, arc understanding (fast middle, slow ends), the five-step safe-ride ritual, and waiting for slow swings before dismounting.

Words to learn

swingchainsseatarcmiddlemountstep off

Say this to your child

“"The swing is a machine with parts! The CHAINS hold, the SEAT carries, and the ARC is the ride — flying between two high corners, fastest in the middle, slow at the ends. And the safe-ride system: mount from the front… hold the chains… pump the legs… slow down… step off. Five steps, every ride — the sky, safely, forever!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the swing — chains, seat, and the flying arc!"
  2. The parts: the CHAINS hold, the SEAT carries, the ARC is the ride — forward high, back high, fast in the middle.
  3. The arc’s secret: the middle is the fast part, the two ends are the slow corners — that is why the ends are the safe places to be.
  4. The safe-ride system: mount from the front, hold the chains, pump the legs, slow down at the end, step off — five steps, every ride.
  5. Play the system game below and close: "mount, hold, pump, slow, step."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Swing" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly swing illustration below — exactly as the chains, seat and arc look.

Ask your child

"Name the swing’s parts. Where is the arc fastest? Say the five safe-ride steps."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Chains, seat, arc!" "Fast in the middle, slow at the corners!" or the system-rider: "Mount, hold, pump, slow, step!"

Out in the real world

Swings hang on every playground with the same three parts — and the five-step system transfers to every swing, rope or boat ride after. Naming the machine is owning the machine.

Try it together

Five-Step Flights: at the swing, say the system aloud as you ride it — "mount… hold… pump… (flying!)… slow… step!" — three full flights with the words pacing the ride. Then the parts quiz: point to the chains, the seat, the arc’s middle. Finish with a slow-corner rest: hang at the back corner, feel how slow and safe the ends are. The machine named, the system ridden, the sky mastered.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the parts. Where are the slow corners? Count the five steps." Chains-seat-arc, the ends, mount-hold-pump-slow-step — three answers and the flight is safe.

Parent tips

Say the five steps WITH the rider — the words are the ritual; rituals are the safety. And the slow-corner rest quietly teaches why the ends are the dismount places.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Tunnel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the tunnel — through the dark and out the other side — with the crawl, the hello-call and the brave truth that tunnels always end in light.

What is this?

A tunnel is a tube to crawl through: dark in the middle, light at both ends — hands and knees forward, a hello echo inside, and the exit always ahead.

What does it mean?

The tunnel is the playground’s tiny bravery lesson: a moment of dark, a voice that echoes, and the proof — every single time — that going THROUGH reaches the other side. That proof is worth more than the crawl.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tunnel ideas: crawl forward on hands and knees — the tunnel is not for standing; the CALL works — hello! echoes down the tube and tells everyone where you are; and tunnels END — keep crawling toward the light; the exit is always ahead.

Why this matters

Dark-tunnel confidence is real courage practice in playground portions — and the echo-call adds voice play, turn-taking and the joy of hearing yourself come back.

What it teaches

Crawling coordination in a confined space, voice-echo play, dark-to-light courage, and the through-to-the-other-side completion.

Words to learn

tunnelcrawldarklightechohellothrough

Say this to your child

“"The tunnel goes through the dark and out the other side! Crawl forward on hands and knees… halfway, call HELLO — hear the echo? The tunnel talks back! And the brave truth of every tunnel: it always ENDS — the light is ahead, keep crawling. Through… echo… light. That is the tunnel’s whole promise!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the tunnel — through the dark, out to the light!"
  2. The crawl: hands and knees, forward — the tunnel is a crawling road, head up enough to see.
  3. The call: halfway in, call HELLO — hear the echo bounce back? The tunnel talks! Calling also tells friends where you are.
  4. The brave truth: tunnels always END — the exit is light, and it is always ahead. Keep crawling; the other side is coming.
  5. Play the tunnel games below and close: "crawl, call, through to the light."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Tunnel" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly tunnel illustration below — exactly as the through-tube looks.

Ask your child

"How do we travel in a tunnel? What does the echo do? What is always ahead in a tunnel?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Hands and knees, crawl!" "HELLO… hello… hello — it echoed!" or the brave one: "Tunnels always end in light!"

Out in the real world

Tunnels curve through every playground — and the through-to-the-light courage transfers to duvets, cardboard boxes and the big world’s underpasses. The echo is free everywhere.

Try it together

Echo Tunnel Run: crawl in, call HELLO at the middle, listen to the bounce, crawl out to the light — arms up: "THROUGH!" Then the two-way round: one crawler at each end, calling echoes to each other, passing with a giggle in the middle. Three throughs, three echoes, one brave ritual. The tunnel’s promise kept, every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we travel? What does the call make? What is always ahead?" Crawl, an echo, the light — three answers and the tunnel is through.

Parent tips

A familiar voice waiting at the EXIT turns dark tunnels into races — the light has a face. And never rush a pause in the middle: waiting in the dark is part of the courage too.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Help — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches help — the helper’s eye: spotting someone who needs a hand, offering BEFORE being asked, and helping in a way that feels kind.

What is this?

Help is giving someone a hand with what they cannot do alone: lifting the heavy bucket, reaching the high bar, picking up the dropped spade — spotted, offered and done kindly.

What does it mean?

Helping is the playground’s quiet hero skill, and it has a craft: the SPOT (look around for the stuck, the dropped, the heavy), the OFFER ("want help?"), and the KIND way (helping WITH, not doing FOR).

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three help ideas: helpers SPOT — eyes scan for someone stuck, dropped or heavy-laden; helpers OFFER first — "want help?" beats grabbing in; and helping is WITH — carry one side of the bucket, don’t take the whole job over.

Why this matters

A playground with helpers is a different playground — and the offer-first habit is the social skill that makes help land as kindness, not takeover.

What it teaches

Awareness of others’ needs, the offer-before-act habit, cooperative carrying, and the feeling of being useful — pride that invites more helping.

Words to learn

helpspotofferhandcarrytogetherkind

Say this to your child

“"Help is the helper’s eye — spotting who needs a hand! Look around: someone is stuck, someone dropped their spade, someone carries something heavy. Walk over and OFFER: ‘Want help?’ Then help WITH — one side of the bucket, one end of the job — helping together, never taking over. Helpers make the whole playground warmer!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is help — the helper’s eye!"
  2. The spot: look around the playground — who is stuck? who dropped something? who carries something heavy? The helper’s eye finds them.
  3. The offer: walk over and ASK — "want help?" Offering first makes help kind.
  4. Helping WITH: carry ONE side of the bucket, hold ONE end of the ladder — helpers share the job, they don’t steal it.
  5. Play the helper games below and close: "spot, offer, help with."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Help" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly helping illustration below — exactly as the offered hand looks.

Ask your child

"What does the helper’s eye do? What do we say before helping? What is helping WITH?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I spotted the stuck one!" "Want help? — I offered first!" or the co-carrier: "I carried one side — helping with!"

Out in the real world

Help moments fill every day: the dropped shopping, the stuck zip, the heavy door — spot, offer, help-with works at every age and every scale. The playground is just the training ground.

Try it together

Helper Scan: walk the playground (or the house) on a helper mission — scan for one thing that needs a hand: a toy on the high shelf, a door, a spilled basket. Offer first, help with, and hear the thank-you. Then the bucket drill: two carriers, one loaded bucket — one side each, walking in step. Three helps a day: the helper’s eye grows on use.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the helper’s eye do? What comes first — offering or grabbing? What is the WITH rule?" Spots, offering, share the job — three answers and the playground warms up.

Parent tips

Praise the OFFER even when help is refused — "great offering!" builds the habit independently of the outcome. And the WITH rule is the kindness core: helpers share jobs, not confiscate them.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Share — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches sharing — the maths of kindness: one toy, two friends, traded time — and the magic sentence that opens every shared game.

What is this?

Share is letting someone use what you have: trading time on the swing, splitting the sand toys, passing the ball — sharing turns one toy into a two-person game.

What does it mean?

Sharing is not losing — it is the trade that makes games bigger: one ball hoarded is one bored child; one ball shared is a catch game. And the share sentence — "want a go?" — is the whole skill in three words.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three share ideas: sharing is TRADED TIME — not giving away forever; the share sentence opens it — "want a go?"; and sharing grows the game — shared toys make shared friends.

Why this matters

The child who shares is never short of playmates — and the traded-time framing (rather than give-it-away) keeps sharing feeling fair, which is why it sticks.

What it teaches

Turn-within-play, the offer sentence, delayed satisfaction (my turn comes back), and the social maths — shared play is bigger play.

Words to learn

sharetradeturnwant a gotogetherfairkind

Say this to your child

“"Sharing is the maths of kindness! It is not giving away — it is TIME TRADES: your go, then my go, then yours again. And the magic sentence is ‘want a go?’ — say it before anyone asks! One ball alone is one game; one ball shared is CATCH — sharing grows the game. Share-first hands have the most friends on the playground."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is share — the maths of kindness!"
  2. Traded time: sharing is not giving away — it is TIME TRADES: your go, then my go, then yours again. Practise the trade out loud.
  3. The share sentence: "want a go?" — three words that open every toy. Say it before being asked: share-first is the superpower version.
  4. The maths: one ball alone is one game; one ball shared is catch, and catch is bigger. Sharing grows the game!
  5. Play the share games below and close: "want a go? — traded time, bigger game."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Share" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly sharing illustration below — exactly as the kind trade looks.

Ask your child

"Is sharing giving away or trading time? What is the magic sentence? What does sharing do to the game?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Traded time — my go comes back!" "Want a go? I said it first!" or the maths fan: "Shared ball = catch game!"

Out in the real world

Shares run every playdate, family and classroom — traded time works for bikes, tablets and swings alike. And share-first is the playground’s fastest friendship strategy.

Try it together

Trade-Clock: one beloved toy, two players. The holder offers — "want a go?" — and the trade happens on a count (ten swings of the swing, ten sandcastles, ten bounces) — then TRADE BACK. The clock makes the return certain, which is what makes sharing safe. Then share-first round: the toy is offered BEFORE any ask. Ten trades, zero grabbing, one very social toy.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is sharing — giving away or trading? Say the magic sentence. What grows when we share?" Trading, "want a go?", the game — three answers and the hands are kind.

Parent tips

The countable trade is the training wheels — certain return teaches generous offering. And praise share-FIRST louder than share-when-asked: the superpower version deserves the spotlight.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Stop — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches stop — the strongest word on the playground, with two jobs: it stops MY body when I say it, and it stops ME when someone else says it.

What is this?

Stop is a full brake, said out loud: "STOP!" freezes a game, a chase, a tickle-fight — and the rule is simple: stop means stop, first time, every time, whoever says it.

What does it mean?

Stop is the playground’s safety word and its fairness word at once: the child who can stop ON COMMAND can play wilder games safely — and the child who RESPECTS others’ stop is trusted with bigger play.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three stop ideas: saying STOP is a power everyone has — your own word, your own brake; respecting STOP is the rule — when anyone says it, everything pauses, first time; and the freeze proves it — a full stop is a statue, not a slowing-down.

Why this matters

Games get wilder and braver when everyone trusts the brake — stop is literally the skill that UNLOCKS rough-and-tumble play, taught as a power and a respect at once.

What it teaches

Impulse control (the freeze on command), respecting others’ boundaries instantly, voice as a safety tool, and the trust that follows a kept stop.

Words to learn

stopfreezebrakerespectpausesafestatue

Say this to your child

“"STOP is the strongest word on the playground — and it has two jobs! Your job: say STOP and your body freezes — statue, mid-game, mid-giggle. Everyone’s job: when anyone says stop, EVERYTHING pauses — first time, no arguing, stop means stop. A playground where stops are honoured is a playground where wild games are safe!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is stop — the strongest word on the playground!"
  2. Your brake: practise saying STOP and freezing your own body — mid-run, mid-dance, mid-giggle. Statue! Your word brakes your body.
  3. The respect rule: when ANYONE says stop — a friend, a small sibling, a grown-up — everything pauses. First time. No bargaining. Stop means stop.
  4. The freeze check: a real stop is a statue — feet planted, hands still. A slowing-down is not a stop.
  5. Play the stop games below and close: "my brake, your brake, stop means stop."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Stop" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly stop illustration below — exactly as the frozen moment looks.

Ask your child

"What are the two jobs of stop? When someone says stop, how many times do we need? What does a real stop look like?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My word brakes my body!" "First time — stop means stop!" or the frozen one: "Statue! Feet planted, hands still!"

Out in the real world

Stops keep every chase, tackle and tickle-fight safe — and the respect rule travels to every game, classroom and family moment after: stop means stop is the treaty of all wild play.

Try it together

Red Light Freeze: run and dance freely until the call — "STOP!" — full statue: feet planted, hands still, three seconds. Vary the caller: sometimes the CHILDREN call stop and the grown-ups freeze too — the rule is for everyone. Then the respect drill: a gentle game (a soft chase) stops the instant ANY player says stop — honoured in one beat, praised by name. My brake, your brake: the strongest word, kept strong.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name stop’s two jobs. How many warnings before stop means stop? What does a real stop look like?" My brake and your brake, zero warnings, a statue — three answers and the games get braver.

Parent tips

The grown-up freezing too is the secret — children believe in stop when they see it honoured upward. And never use stop as a punisher: it is a safety tool and must stay glamorous.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Take Turns — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches taking turns — the fair machine: my go, your go, a queue everyone can see, and waiting that turns into watching.

What is this?

Take turns is trading goes: my turn, then your turn, in an order everyone can see — the queue, the count, the next-up — so every game with one swing, one spade or one spotlight stays fair.

What does it mean?

Turn-taking is fairness made visible: the queue shows the order, the count shows the length, and next-up shows the hope. Children wait bravely when the system is SEEABLE — which is why queues, timers and turn-tokens work.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three turn ideas: turns are an ORDER everyone can see — the queue or the count; my go ends and YOURS begins — the handover is part of the turn; and waiting is easier when watching — the next turner learns the game while they wait.

Why this matters

Turn-taking runs every classroom, every family and every queue on Earth — taught here at the slide and the swing, where the fairness is felt in the body.

What it teaches

Queue patience, handover rituals (my go ends cleanly), watching-to-learn while waiting, and fairness perception — the seen order soothes.

Words to learn

take turnsmy goyour goqueuenext uphandoverfair

Say this to your child

“"Taking turns is the fair machine! Turns work when everyone can SEE them: the queue, the count, the next-up name. My go ends with a handover — ‘YOUR go!’ — clean and loud. And waiting is easier when it is watching: the waiter learns the whole game before their turn. My go, your go, next up — fair, seen, fun!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is take turns — the fair machine!"
  2. The seen order: turns work when everyone can SEE them — a queue, a count, a next-up name. Hidden turns feel unfair; seen turns feel fair.
  3. The handover: my go ends with a handover — "your go!" — clean and loud. A tidy handover is half the fairness.
  4. Waiting watches: the waiter watches the rider — learning the game, spotting the tricks. Waiting is practising.
  5. Play the turn games below and close: "my go, your go, next up!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Take Turns" stand in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly turn-taking illustration below — exactly as the fair queue looks.

Ask your child

"What makes turns FEEL fair — seen or hidden? What ends my go? What does the waiter do while waiting?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Seen turns are fair turns!" "YOUR go! — I handed over clean!" or the watcher: "I learned the trick while I waited!"

Out in the real world

Turns run every classroom turn-and-talk, every board game, every family bathroom queue — and the handover ritual works everywhere. Waiting-while-watching even makes waiting useful.

Try it together

Turn-Token Queue: one swing, three players — each holds a token (a leaf, a cap); the swing belongs to the token-holder, and the handover is the token pass: "YOUR go!" Countable goes (ten pushes) keep the length fair. The waiters watch-and-learn one trick per wait. Rotate until every token has flown twice. Seen order, clean handovers, useful waiting: the fair machine, fully running.

Understanding check

Ask: "What makes turns fair? What ends my go? What does waiting become?" Seen order, the handover, watching — three answers and the queue hums along.

Parent tips

Make the handover a CELEBRATION — "your go!" with a grin turns the end of my fun into the start of ours. And countable goes beat vague ones: certain length teaches certain waiting.

PLAYGROUND LESSON · PLAYGROUND · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Wait — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches waiting — the brave pause: holding still while the good thing comes, with a trick that makes the waiting smaller: watching.

What is this?

Wait is pausing with patience: the queue, the count-down, the pause before the story starts — hands and feet that hold while the good thing comes closer.

What does it mean?

Waiting is the hardest and most useful skill on the playground — and it shrinks when it is COUNTABLE (how long?) and WATCHABLE (what is happening?). The brave pause is not empty time; it is time with a shape.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three wait ideas: waiting has a SHAPE — a count, a number of whooshes, a song’s length — shaped waiting is small waiting; the body holds — hands busy (counting, squeezing) and feet planted; and watching shrinks waiting — the waiter who watches is already half-playing.

Why this matters

Waiting is the gateway skill to classrooms, queues and conversations for life — and the count-and-watch trick makes it a game the child can win today.

What it teaches

Patience with shape (countable waits), stillness with busy hands, watching-as-participation, and the celebration of waited-for things.

Words to learn

waitpausecountshapeholdwatchpatience

Say this to your child

“"Waiting is the brave pause — and it has tricks! Give the wait a SHAPE: count the whooshes, sing the waiting song, count down from ten. Give the hands a job and the feet a spot. And watch the game you’re waiting for — the waiter who watches is already half-playing! Shaped waiting is small waiting. The good thing always comes."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is wait — the brave pause!"
  2. The shape: waiting shrinks when it has a shape — count the whooshes, sing the song, count down from ten. Name the shape before waiting starts.
  3. The body holds: hands get a JOB (count on fingers, squeeze a pocket) and feet get a SPOT (planted, planted, planted).
  4. Watching trick: watch the rider, the builder, the game — the waiter who watches is half-playing already, and the wait halves.
  5. Play the wait games below and close: "shape, hold, watch."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Wait" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly waiting illustration below — exactly as the brave pause looks.

Ask your child

"What shrinks a wait — a shape or empty time? What jobs do the hands get? What does watching do to waiting?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I counted the whooshes!" "My hands counted, my feet planted!" or the watcher: "I watched — the wait halved!"

Out in the real world

Waits fill every day: the kettle, the traffic light, the turn at the tap — and the count-and-watch trick works on all of them. Children who can wait at four can learn anything at five.

Try it together

Count-Down Waits: at the swing, slide or any queue — the waiter picks the shape (ten pushes, three whooshes, one song) and the count is public. Hands count on fingers, feet hold the spot, eyes watch the game. When the turn arrives — big cheer, because WAITED-FOR things are the best things. Three waits, three shapes, one brave pauser. The good thing comes — every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "What gives a wait its shape? What are the hands’ and feet’s jobs? What does the watcher become?" The count, count-and-plant, half-playing — three answers and the pause is brave.

Parent tips

Always name the shape BEFORE the wait starts — unshaped waiting is where meltdowns live. And celebrate the waited-for arrival loudly: waiting earns the best applause.

This lesson pairs with the Wait flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Playground.
